generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this approach shows up in how you meet each piece of work, not in a one-off decision. You treat a task as a chance to grow, trust that effort and good strategies will help, and study to understand rather than only to score. Brought to every module, the three ideas become one steady way of working.
generatedProse.worked-example: Two students begin the same module. One aims only at the mark, picks safe topics, and treats ability as fixed, so a hard task feels like a threat. The other treats the module as a chance to grow, trusts that effort will pay off, and chooses the topic worth understanding. Over the term the second student learns more and grows more, because the three ideas worked together as one approach.
generatedProse.summary: These three ideas are strongest when you use them together. You treat work as a chance to grow, meet it believing effort pays off, and study to understand, again and again across your modules. It is this joined-up approach, not any single idea, that helps you start well and keep improving.

check.body: A student takes on a harder module topic to understand it better, believes they can improve with effort, and treats the work as a chance to grow rather than only a grade. What does this show?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first essay, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next essay.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using feedback to plan the next piece of work feeds it straight back into your learning, closing the loop and starting the next round stronger. That is the cycle working as it should.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student did with the feedback, and what improved as a result.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Acting on feedback feeds your next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay was stronger. The mark on the first essay cannot change, but the feedback still shapes what comes next.

_items.text: The three ideas working as one approach: learning motivation, self-belief and excelling together.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three are at work in how this student approaches the task.
Choosing the harder topic to understand it is learning motivation, not performance motivation.
Believing they can improve with effort is a growth mindset, not a fixed one.
The student treats the work as a chance to grow, which is more than chasing marks.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
